newsitem.title: USA: Aninat - economic reformers must weigh social costs.
newsitem.headline: Aninat - economic reformers must weigh social costs.

text.p: Chile's Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat said Wednesday that policymakers needed to weigh carefully the social costs of economic adjustment lest they lose popular support for reform.

Aninat, who acted as chairman of the IMF/World Bank meetings underway here, told reporters that developing countries should consider social effects such as unemployment wrought by opening up to the global economy.

"In any country if you produce a very purist macro-economic adjustment and discount the social effects, you may end up without political support," he said, calling for a 'bridge' between tough macroeconomic plans and the building of political support to make economic reform more enduring.

Chile's economic reforms over the past decade have brought sustained high economic growth, lower inflation and higher savings and the efforts are widely considered to be a model for developing nations.

This perspective is reflected in a new philosophy at the International Monetary Fund, which often makes its loans to developing nations conditional on their progress in economic liberalization, the Chilean minister said.
"The IMF is speaking more and more of the issue of employment, of the quality of employment, and the quality of the adjustment," Aninat said.
The Fund was placing emphasis on the social effects of economic adjustment, discarding the approach that any kind of free markets would be positive, Aninat said.

Part of the challenge that governments face to provide jobs stemmed from rapid technological advances, which are forcing dramatic changes in labor. "The world is leading a silent revolution in technology," he said. "This is producing a lot of restructuring of employment.'

Many economists consider Chile's imposition of capital controls, or transaction fees, which placed heavy costs on short term foreign capital flows, to have been a key element to Chile's successful transformation to a market economy.
But the minister offerred little advice to other developing nations about the controls, which he credited as providing stability to Chile following Mexico's financial crisis last year.
"We do not plan to export it as a device to other countries," Aninat said. "Each country has to make its own decision.'
